item.title: Beyond Symptom Relief: Psychodynamic Therapy for Anxiety
item.description:
Anxiety

Beyond Symptom Relief: Psychodynamic Therapy for Anxiety

Understanding anxiety’s roots can help create lasting change.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety often carries meanings rooted in personal history, relationships, and emotional conflict.
  • Psychodynamic therapy explores what anxiety protects against or struggles to communicate.
  • Greater emotional awareness can soften anxiety and expand our freedom to choose.

People generally use the word anxiety to refer to their feelings of excessive worry, fear, restlessness, or physical arousal. Most of my patients understand that “rationally” their fears are disproportionate or that there is no evidence of the catastrophe they fear, yet continue living in a state of alarm.

Anxiety may persist because it is not simply an “error” or a “distortion” in our thinking, but a meaningful response within our larger emotional life. Anxiety is created less by an external cause and more by our internal reaction to it and, in that way, it is tied to who we are and to our personal history.

Psychodynamic therapy approaches anxiety with curiosity. Rather than treating it only as something to eliminate or “fix,” it helps us understand what the anxiety is trying to protect or communicate. This does not mean that anxiety is consciously chosen, but that change can be more lasting when we understand why we seem to operate in a constant state of alarm.

Anxiety has an inner history

Anxiety is often rooted in the present and the past at the same time. A difficult meeting, a period of uncertainty, or tension with someone close can activate emotional reactions that were formed much earlier in life. Reactions that once were adaptive and may have helped us preserve a sense of connection or safety can later in life make ordinary uncertainty feel intolerable.

Often, the immediate worry is not the whole story. For example, a fear of failure may carry concerns about shame, exposure, dependence, or the loss of love.

Anxiety can also protect us against emotions that feel harder to bear directly: anger toward someone we need, grief over what has been lost, longing, envy, or a painful sense of vulnerability. Psychodynamic anxiety therapy can offer a space to recognize these feelings and what makes them so intolerable.

Making room for what anxiety conceals

There is a misconception that psychodynamic therapy is confined to analyzing the past. The reality is that it also involves developing greater capacity to experience difficult emotions without immediately converting them into worry, urgency, avoidance, or self-criticism.

As underlying feelings, conflicts, wishes, and longings become more recognizable and speakable, they are less likely to require anxiety as their messenger. The work may also address the automatic habits that keep anxiety in place: relentless self-monitoring, an unconscious demand for certainty, or the belief that vigilance prevents loss.

It is only natural that some of these emotional patterns will emerge in the work with a therapist. Some of my patients may be worried about disappointing me, hesitant to express their reactions towards me, or particularly sensitive to a moment of silence or a change in tone.

Psychodynamic anxiety therapy takes these moments not as distractions or as problems, but as feelings that have meaning. A skilled therapist will see them as opportunities to collaboratively examine, in real time, how anxiety emerges in relationship with ourselves and others.

A different relationship to uncertainty

Psychodynamic anxiety therapy does not promise a life without anxiety. Some anxiety is a natural and useful response to uncertainty, change, responsibility, and the fact that we cannot fully control the people we love or the future we imagine.

Its goal is not to replace concern with indifference, but to help people distinguish present danger from older emotional expectations. Over time, the grip of anxiety can become gentler. You can feel apprehension without assuming a catastrophic outcome, recognize familiar, old fears without having them organize your whole life, and make room for wishes and conflicts that had previously been experienced only as a signal of alarm.

In this sense, psychodynamic anxiety therapy helps not only by reducing symptoms, but by making one’s inner life more intelligible, more bearable, and more available for choice.

item.title: Father of Georgia Shooter Will Spend 15 Years in Prison
item.description:
Psychiatry

Father of Georgia Shooter Will Spend 15 Years in Prison

A recent sentencing reinforces the glaring need for prevention strategies.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Legal precedent grows as parents face prison for negligence in child-perpetrated school shootings.
  • Ignoring warning signs and allowing access to weapons can result in criminal charges for parents.
  • Preventive mental health interventions, including warrants or hospitalization, can help avert tragedies.

On July 30, Colin Gray, father of Colt Gray, who killed four people in a 2024 school shooting, was sentenced to 15 years in prison, marking the third time a parent has been prosecuted for a murder committed by a child in their care.

Source: Milad Fakurian / Unsplash

The sentence, which comes after the similar prosecution of Jennifer and James Crumbley of Michigan, reinforces a growing legal precedent of holding parents criminally responsible when their negligence contributes to a minor child perpetrating such an act.

Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm, who delivered the sentence, conveyed this clearly, acknowledging from the bench that Mr. Gray had no criminal history and did not intend to commit a crime. Still, he acknowledged that the defendant ignored glaring warning signs, including his son’s history of violent episodes and threatening social media posts, even permitting him to keep a firearm in his room.

“It became more and more obvious that something bad was going to happen,” said the judge. “At a minimum, you should have believed that Colt would commit suicide. And you failed to do the simplest things to prevent this.”

As a family-focused mental health attorney, I find the judge’s words particularly poignant, because proactive preventive measures are indeed crucial in these situations. As a first step, parents must eliminate their child’s access to weapons, and then reach out to qualified professionals to recommend potential legal avenues, including:

  • Psychiatric intervention: Distinct from those featured in movies and TV shows, psychiatric interventions bring together a specialized team of practitioners, along with concerned family members, to address someone’s escalating mental health issues. With a mental health attorney, psychiatrist, case manager, and often security personnel, loved ones can best ensure an individual in crisis, who lacks the capacity to understand their condition, receives the help they require.
  • Hospitalization: An individual can be hospitalized voluntarily or involuntarily if an episode occurs in which the individual poses a substantial risk of harm to self and/or others. Psychiatric hospitalization allows for a psychiatrist and/or other mental health professional to evaluate any potential medical and mental health issues, establish a diagnosis, and recommend a treatment plan.
  • Mental health warrant: The process of obtaining a mental health warrant involves petitioning the court to issue a civil warrant to bring the individual, with appointed counsel, to court for a hearing. Here, the court determines if he/she currently poses a danger to self or others and should be remanded to a psychiatric emergency room for immediate evaluation and possible admission for treatment.

Of course, a family’s options change considerably once a child turns 18 years old and is considered an adult in the eyes of the law. This milestone—or its approach—should prompt family members to consider the items above and then explore additional measures, including:

  • Guardianship or conservatorship: This proceeding authorizes the court to appoint and oversee a legal decision-maker for another adult, who, due to incapacity, disability, or “functional limitations,” is unable to manage his/her own affairs.
  • Assisted Outpatient Treatment (AOT): This court-ordered treatment for an adult’s mental illness and supervision in the community aims to prevent “a relapse or deterioration,” as well as the “revolving door” we often see in these cases.
  • Advance directives: Legal advance directive documents, executed while the individual has the requisite mental capacity, contain an individual’s prior expressed wishes regarding medical treatment or financial affairs. They include such documents as health care proxies and powers of attorney.
  • HIPAA and state-specific release forms: Filling out the proper authorization allows treatment providers to release otherwise confidential information pertaining to patients/clients to family members or other designated individuals. This makes it possible for families to speak with treatment teams and best understand diagnoses and medical or psychiatric treatment records, as well as actively participate in discharge planning.

These options, part of a mental health toolkit, might not be well known among families, but they should be top of mind for mental health practitioners as well as educators, law enforcement, EMTs, and other professionals who are increasingly serving as first responders for those experiencing mental health crises. Greater awareness can go a long way towards helping to prevent such tragedies and the terrible consequences they inflict on individuals and communities.

item.title: Sexsomnia: What We Know About Sexual Behaviors During Sleep
item.description:
Sleep

Sexsomnia: What We Know About Sexual Behaviors During Sleep

Sexual behaviors during sleep are getting more clinical and medical attention.

Posted August 20, 2026

Key points
  • Sexsomnia involves sexual behaviors during sleep that are typically not remembered in the morning.
  • As much as 10 percent of a general population may experience sexsomnia, and it is more common in men.
  • Because most people don't remember the behaviors, diagnosis can be complex.
Source: StockSnap/Pixabay

Sexsomnia can sound improbable: A person may initiate sexual activity, masturbate, touch a partner, or attempt intercourse while asleep—and have little or no memory of it the next morning. Yet it is a recognized sleep phenomenon.

Sexsomnia is generally considered a non-rapid eye movement (NREM) parasomnia, in the same family as sleepwalking, sleep terrors, and confusional arousals. Despite growing recognition, much remains unknown, and there is no standardized sexsomnia-specific diagnostic test.

What happens during sexsomnia?

Sexsomnia does not refer to sexual dreams or simply having a sexual response, such as an erection or nocturnal emission (wet dreams) while asleep. Instead, it involves sexual behaviors arising during sleep. Reported behaviors range from masturbation and pelvic thrusting to fondling of a bedmate, sexual vocalizations, attempts to initiate intercourse, and, less commonly, completed intercourse.

A central feature is impaired awareness. People experiencing sexsomnia may be difficult to wake or respond poorly to someone speaking to them. If awakened, they may seem confused or disoriented. Afterwards, they typically have no memory of what happened, although some people have fragmentary recall.

Because people often learn about episodes from a partner, sexsomnia can cause embarrassment, guilt, and relationship difficulties, as well as serious concerns about consent and safety.

How common is sexsomnia?

For years, prevalence was difficult to estimate because most research involved people attending sleep clinics rather than the general population, leaving out all the people who experience this and never seek treatment. Sexsomnia may also be underreported because of embarrassment, stigma, and the fact that people who sleep alone may simply be unaware of their behavior.

Recent population research suggests it may be less rare than previously assumed. For years, prevalence was difficult to estimate because most research involved sleep-clinic patients, while embarrassment and lack of awareness may contribute to underreporting.

A 2025 Norwegian study of 1,002 adults found that 10.5 percent reported having experienced sexsomnia at some point in their lives and 6.1 percent within the previous three months. Men had about 1.6 times the odds of reporting lifetime sexsomnia compared with women, consistent with the male predominance seen in clinical reports. However, sex was not significantly associated with recent sexsomnia.

These figures require caution. The study relied on self-report rather than clinical diagnosis and did not confirm episodes through sleep studies or partner reports. Most reported episodes were also relatively infrequent. A very small percentage of people reported experiencing sexsomnia episodes on a weekly basis. Masturbation was the most commonly reported specific behavior, and completed intercourse was extremely rare.

Source: DieterRobbins/Pixabay

What causes it?

Sexsomnia is best understood as a problem of partial awakening rather than a disorder of sexuality.

One leading explanation is “state dissociation.” Normally, the brain transitions between sleep and wakefulness in a coordinated way. During an NREM parasomnia, that transition may be incomplete. Motor and emotional brain systems can become sufficiently activated to produce surprisingly complex behavior while regions involved in judgment, self-awareness, and memory remain relatively “asleep.” Some of these same mechanisms appear to drive behaviors such as sleepwalking.

Sexsomnia also commonly overlaps with other parasomnias, including sleepwalking, sleep terrors, and confusional arousals.

Potential triggers include sleep deprivation, stress, irregular sleep schedules, alcohol, and medications that affect sleep. Conditions that repeatedly disturb sleep—particularly obstructive sleep apnea—may also provoke partial arousals in susceptible people. Physical contact with a bed partner can sometimes precipitate an episode as well.

These are best regarded as possible precipitating factors rather than simple causes. For example, millions of people experience sleep deprivation without developing sexsomnia.

How is sexsomnia evaluated?

There is no single blood test, brain scan, or overnight sleep measurement that can prove someone has sexsomnia. Diagnosis therefore depends on identifying a pattern of evidence.

Clinicians ask what happened, when and how often episodes occur, whether the person responds during them, and what they remember afterwards. They also assess other parasomnias, sleep patterns, stress, alcohol, medications, and possible sleep disorders.

Information from a bed partner or other witness can be particularly valuable because the person experiencing sexsomnia may have no memory of the event. Witnesses can describe the behavior, responsiveness, difficulty waking the person, and whether snoring, abnormal breathing, or other signs of disturbed sleep occurred beforehand.

What else could it be?

Diagnosis also means considering alternative explanations.

REM sleep behavior disorder can cause people to physically act out dreams, but it arises from REM rather than NREM sleep and is often associated with vivid dream recall. Sleep-related epilepsy can produce unusual movements—including occasionally sexual behaviors—but seizures tend to be brief, repetitive, and highly stereotyped. Medication or substance effects, intoxication, and other neurological or psychiatric conditions may also need consideration.

An overnight video-polysomnogram, or sleep study, can help identify conditions such as sleep apnea or epilepsy. However, sexsomnia episodes are rarely captured in the sleep laboratory, so a normal study does not rule out the condition.

Source: Myléne/Pixabay

A diagnosis built from the whole picture

Sexsomnia should not be diagnosed from one unusual nighttime event. Assessment considers the behavior, awareness and memory, personal and family parasomnia history, possible triggers, witness accounts, medical and medication history, and testing when needed to exclude other explanations.

The science is still developing, and there is no validated sexsomnia-specific interview, rating scale, or sleep-study marker. Better population studies and diagnostic tools should help clarify who is most vulnerable and improve clinicians' ability to diagnose the condition confidently.
